She wrote, "I desire you would remember the ladies and be more generous and favorable to them than your ancestors. Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of the husbands." It could be hard to convince the non-adventurous eater to choose a chewy sesame ball of dough floating in water over an ice cream sundae, or a red-bean dumpling over a decadent chocolate cake. However, as someone with Taiwanese roots who grew up in Australia eating these Asian desserts, I personally would fight for the last bite of tang yuan , zongzi or a mooncake if given a chance. During the Mid-Autumn Festival, or Moon Festival, celebrated by Chinese around the world on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month each year (September 17 this year), mooncakes are eaten in gluttonous quantities. By mid-August, supermarkets, grocery stores, bakeries and even luxury hotels stockpile the desserts to cater to mooncake madness—an industry valued at more than $2.3 billion in recent years. Families gather together over a meal and light lanterns, look at the moon and eat yue bing , otherwise known as mooncakes, wishing each other wealth and happiness. Adams had died in 2002, a year before Cummings’ retirement, but Cummings became fascinated with her story—and with that of the 6888th Central Postal Directory Battalion, the unit Adams had commanded. It was the only unit composed entirely of Black women to have been deployed overseas during the war , and it had served a critical function: clearing the backlog of mail that marked the only line of communication between American soldiers in Europe and their loved ones back home. The officers and enlisted women of the Six Triple Eight had been given a difficult mission, and they’d succeeded. pages.title: The Remarkable, Amazing Stories of Route 66 Reflect the Twists and Turns of 100 Years of Americana
pages.description: Among the first interstates, the beloved roadway that connected Chicago to Los Angeles still looms large in popular culture and our collective imagination
pages.text: The Remarkable, Amazing Stories of Route 66 Reflect the Twists and Turns of 100 Years of Americana Skip to main content There's More to That A Smithsonian magazine special report Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Images via Library of Congress and public domain The famed Route 66 has had many lives . It emerged in an era when cars were new but roads were dangerous and intended for horses. But there were those who imagined a highway that would connect the cities of the Midwest to the West Coast — and Route 66 was born. During the Great Depression, the roadway helped migrants find their way to new jobs in the West. During World War II, it facilitated the transportation of munitions and armaments en route to the Pacific theater. Later, it became a busy thoroughfare for Americans wanting to explore their country. Storefronts, towns, gas stations, cafes and much more grew up along its edges. Then, as major interstates became the main byways for traveling Americans, Route 66 fell into obsolescence, becoming more a time capsule than roadway. Today, some of those roadside stops still exist, catering to tourists seeking a dose of unvarnished Americana. This episode chronicles the origin of the federal interstate system and how Route 66 fits into that history — before the massive tangle of highways and roads we know today were paved and packed with traffic. pages.title: The Rise and Fall of the Great American Motel
pages.description: Mom and pop motels once dominated American highways. Now, they're an endangered species
pages.text: The Rise and Fall of the Great American Motel Skip to main content The Wigwam Motel in Holbrook, Arizona, is one of the few remnants of America’s mid-20th century motel boom. Library of Congress In 1939, when John Steinbeck imagined Highway 66 as “the road of flight,” he evoked the crushing realities of Depression-era migrants who’d been pushed off their land by failing crops, relentless dust and heartless banks. Struggling to find some sense of home on the road, these environmental and economic refugees searched for hope against a backdrop of unfathomable loss. On the road to California, they’d rest and recuperate in army surplus tents, hastily constructed Department of Transportation camps and Sears Roebuck chicken-coop cabins . They could hardly imagine the surreal indulgences of the tourist road that would begin to emerge after World War II: renting a room built to resemble a country cottage and adorned with plastic flowers; snapping photos of a neon cactus glowing through half-drawn window shades; sleeping in a concrete tepee appropriated from Native American culture. They could, in short, never foresee the rise of the roadside motel. But after its heyday in the mid-20th century, the traditional mom and pop motel – once ubiquitous along American highways and byways – has largely slipped from the public imagination. Today’s road-tripper generally prefers lodging that boasts a professional website, guarantees a fast internet connection and promises easy-on-easy-off interstate access, leaving the older motels built along two-lane roads and numbered highways to go to seed.

pages.text: The secret lives of forgotten ancient Greeks | National Geographic By Candida Moss Published July 31, 2026 Stones & Bones is back! Today, we visit an excavation underway in Greece that may reshape what we know about its ancient past. Want to make sure you get every Stones & Bones newsletter? Put your email here . More than two millennia ago, young girls from the Greek countryside used to travel every four years to the Sanctuary of Artemis at Brauron outside Athens, to participate in a mysterious rite of passage. They went there, one ancient participant enigmatically said, to “play the bear.” Guided by the priestesses of Artemis and out of sight of their fathers and brothers, the girls ran free, embodying the bear as part of a ritual that allowed them to shed their wildness and prepare for marriage. Painted cups found at the site that were possibly made by participants themselves show girls running and dancing. They would return later in life to dedicate offerings to the goddess in preparation for childbirth. One day in the third century B.C., the sanctuary was abandoned forever. And no one knows why. Now, a team of British and Greek archaeologists, paleontologists, and other scientists jointly working as part of the ARTEMIS project want to understand not just what those girls were up to and why the sanctuary was abandoned but also what life in rural Brauron was really like for the ordinary inhabitants of ancient Greece. pages.description: When King Henry VIII's wife Anne Boleyn was executed in 1536, her Book of Hours went missing for centuries. A recent discovery reveals a string of women who secured the book for decades after her death.
pages.text: The secrets hidden in Anne Boleyn’s Book of Hours | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE This book vanished when Anne Boleyn was executed. Now it reveals her secrets. When King Henry VIII's wife Anne Boleyn was executed in 1536, her Book of Hours went missing for centuries. A recent discovery reveals a string of women who secured the book for decades after her death. Ultraviolet light reveals writing invisible to the naked eye in the margins of Anne Boleyn’s Book of Hours. The doomed queen’s prayer book disappeared after her execution in 1536 and reappeared around 1903. Photograph courtesy Hever Castle & Gardens By Leslie Patrick Published August 1, 2023 Anne Boleyn, King Henry VIII's second queen, is often portrayed as a seductress and ultimately the woman responsible for changing the face of religion in England. In reality she was a fiercely intelligent and pious woman dedicated to education and religious reform. But after her arrest and execution on false charges of adultery and incest in May 1536, Henry VIII was determined to forget her memory. Her royal emblems were removed from palace walls, her sparkling jewels tucked away in dark coffers, and her precious books disappeared from the pages of time. One of Boleyn’s books that has reappeared is a Book of Hours: The stunning prayer book, printed around 1527 with devotional texts designed to be read throughout the day, features hand-painted woodcuts—as well as a rare example of the queen’s own writing. pages.text: The Species That Domesticated Itself | National Geographic SCIENCE LAELAPS The Species That Domesticated Itself By Riley Black Published December 1, 2009 • 6 min read The skull of Paranthropus boisei (“Zinj,” “Dear Boy,” “Nutcracker Man,” etc.). Louis Leakey had a problem. During the summer of 1959 he and his wife Mary recovered the skull fragments of an early human scattered about the fossil deposits of Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania. The skull had been deposited among the shattered bones of fossil mammals and a collection stone tools, and this led Louis to conclude that it was one of our early ancestors. Only an ancestor of Homo sapiens could be a toolmaker, Louis thought, but the skull looked nothing like that of our species. When Mary fit all the pieces of the fossil puzzle together she and Louis were greeted with a visage that was both familiar and alien. The a low-domed skull capped a face expanded sideways by massive cheek bones through which powerful muscles attached to the jaw. Overall the new skull, affectionately dubbed the “Dear Boy”, was most similar to the skull of the australopithecines from South Africa, specifically a heavy-jawed type called Paranthropus that had been discovered decades before. Louis recognized this similarity, but while he pushed Paranthropus to the sidelines of human evolution he presented the new fossil, named Zinjanthropus , as one of our ancestors. pages.text: The Surprising Secret Weapon Against Spotted Lanternflies | National Geographic Premium ANIMALS The Surprising Secret Weapon Against Spotted Lanternflies Early research suggests that a backyard plant might poison the invasive species. Scientists are studying a promising way to control the spread of the invasive spotted lanternfly with a common plant. Mark Mirko, Connecticut Public/Getty Images By Jason Bittel Published September 1, 2026 The spotted lanternfly is a large, visually striking insect that first showed up in the U.S. in 2014. In just over a decade, this invasive species has multiplied across the American Northeast, with new range expansions into the Midwest and South, bringing the total number of states where they can now be found to 19, as well as the District of Columbia. Not only do they feed on plant sap and harm trees, but spotted lanternflies also pose a threat to the grape and wine industry , among many other crops. Scientists have recently said that squashing them likely won’t make a dent in their populations. However, they may have stumbled upon a new weapon in the fight against the invasive species—one that just so happens to be critical habitat for monarch butterflies , an insect species perhaps as loved as the lanternfly is despised: Milkweed. When spotted lanternflies feed on the stuff, they have a tendency to drop dead. “We were planning to run the experiment for a week, except when we went back the next day, the majority of the lanternflies that were on milkweed were dead,” says Anne Johnson , a postdoctoral researcher at Michigan State University.

pages.text: The Teeth That Changed the Story of Human Evolution | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE FROM THE VAULT The Teeth That Changed the Story of Human Evolution In East Africa in the 1990s, Meave Leakey and the Hominid Gang discovered apelike creatures who walked upright four million years ago. Ape, hominid, or something in between? Based on the shape of the embedded tooth, some researchers believe that a 5.6-million-year-old jaw fragment discovered at Lothagam in 1967 is the oldest hominid fossil yet found. Skeptics say the fragment is too meager to classify. Other finds, in the 1970s, have been identified as specimens of the early hominid Australopithecus afarensis : a partial skeleton called Lucy from Hadar in Ethiopia and a 3.5-million year-old mandible from Tanzania exhumed by the author's mother-in-law, Mary Leakey. With the 1994 Turkana expedition the horizon was pushed back another 600,000 years. Meanwhile, research in Ethiopia by Tim White of the University of California, Berkeley, has uncovered even older fossils, which he has identified as a new genus, Ardipithecus . pages.text: The Treasures Emerging From Turkey’s Dying Lakes | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE The Treasures Emerging From Turkey’s Dying Lakes Climate change is exposing once-submerged churches, castles and petroglyphs—and threatening their survival. The Basilica of Saint Neophytos, the likely site of early Christianity's Nicene Council, used to be submerged beneath Lake İznik. But drought has caused the lake's waters to recede, exposing the ancient structure. Sercan Ozkurnazl, Getty Images By Katie Nadworny Published September 24, 2026 Mustafa Şahin used to spend much more of his time below water. As the founder of Turkey’s first underwater archaeology department, he practiced his work in the country’s lakes, diving deep to uncover important historical ruins. In 2014, he found the Basilica of Saint Neophytos—a contender for the home of the original Nicene Council —in Lake İznik, a discovery that Archaeology Magazine and The Archaeological Institute of America deemed one of the most important that year. But Mustafa isn’t diving anymore. His work as head archaeologist of the basilica now keeps him out of the lake, because Saint Neophytos is no longer under İznik’s waters. It sits on dry ground. Lake İznik is facing a crisis and it isn’t alone. Turkey is losing most of its lakes at an alarming rate: close to 75 percent are in the process of disappearing, many within the last decade. pages.text: The tree nobody liked | National Geographic By Rick Gore Photographs by Bianca Lavies Published April 9, 2026 This story originally published in the May 1977 issue of National Geographic magazine. See more digitized stories from our archives here . I still recall the dredges and the bulldozers working in the red mangrove swamps near my father's house. I never thought their destruction was much of a loss. Mangroves were scrub: junk trees. The peculiar aerial roots, which, like spidery legs, prop the mangroves up in the mud, made the swamps seem forbidding. Swarms of mosquitoes and clicking, crablike creatures lurked within. The mud often stank. "No one likes the mangroves," John Steinbeck once wrote. And in Florida, until very recently, he was right. Few people complained as stands of mangroves along the state's southeast coast were replaced with sea-walled housing developments, hotels, and shopping plazas. Today most of Florida's red mangroves are part of a lush fringe extending along the southern Gulf Coast. They embrace the Ten Thousand Islands, wrap around Everglades National Park, and reach to the tip of the Florida Keys. In the past few years the red mangrove has made a lot of friends. "It is the sacred tree of Florida," says Bill Merrihue of Naples, president of the Collier County Conservancy. Sacred enough for a Miami federal judge to order a trailer-park developer in the Keys to restore to its natural state a mangrove swamp he had dredged without proper permit. pages.text: The Volkswagen Beetle Says Auf Wiedersehen Skip to main content The VW Beetle is retiring Wikimedia /CC BY-SA 2.0 DE The last ever Volkswagen Beetle is rolling off the production line in Puebla, Mexico, today, before heading to go on display at a nearby Volkswagen museum, David McHugh at the Associated Press reports. While car models arrive and disappear each year (take, for instance, the Ford Fiesta , Chevy Cruze and Daimler’s all-electric Smart Car, all of which are also ending production in 2019), few vehicles traveled the long, strange road of the Beetle—often lovingly known as the Bug—which originated out of Nazi Germany and later came to personify the peace-and-love ethos of the 1960s. When Adolf Hitler became chancellor in 1933, he wanted to create a rugged, affordable automobile that would spread car ownership “to the people” throughout the German Reich. In 1938, he was poised to do so, as the Nazis geared up for the mass production of what was then known as the KdF-Wagen—an abbreviation of Kraft durch Freude , literally making it the "Strength Through Joy" car (the name was associated with a larger state-run leisure initiative ). pages.text: There's a Critical Window in Your 50s for Preserving Body Strength | National Geographic Premium HEALTH There's a Critical Window in Your 50s for Preserving Body Strength The fight against frailty can begin decades before physical decline becomes obvious. A new study suggests that biological changes linked to frailty may accelerate at two particular ages in midlife. But researchers have uncovered ways to preserve strength and independence into the twilight years. Rebecca Hale, NGM Staff By Hadia Zainab Published November 4, 2026 Frailty may seem like a problem for old age. But the biological changes that make us more vulnerable to physical decline can begin decades before the first signs appear. A 2026 study in Cell Metabolism analyzed data from more than 50,000 people and found that changes in proteins associated with frailty clustered around two ages: roughly 50 and 63. These molecular patterns may help scientists understand how frailty develops before physical signs appear. Researchers also developed a protein-based frailty score that could eventually help identify people at risk, although more research is needed before it can be used clinically. Around age 50, many of the changes involved proteins related to how the body uses and stores energy and regulates hormones. Visit the Cairngorms in winter and you’ll find a landscape in slumber. The mountains seem to rest wearily beneath the low, mottled clouds, the morning frosts picking out the branches of ancient Scots pines. Yet, this seemingly sleepy time of year hums with life. The Cairngorms National Park, the UK’s largest, is home to a quarter of the country’s rare and endangered species, making it ideal for spotting everything from red squirrels and pine martens to golden eagles and mountain hares. Artwork By Craig Williams © The Trustees of the British Museum By Tom Metcalfe Published December 10, 2025 Archaeologists have discovered what may be the earliest evidence of deliberate fire-making. At a site called East Farm in England, recent excavations revealed reddened silt, flint handaxes distorted by heat, and fragments of a mineral—iron pyrite—that could have been used to make sparks on tinder. Taken together, the finds suggest that an early group of Neanderthals deliberately and repeatedly set fires in a hearth there roughly 400,000 years ago. "In over 36 years of field work and geological studies in the area, we've never found pyrite before," says British Museum archaeologist Nick Ashton , the senior author of a study of the discoveries published in the journal Nature on December 10. "And now, the only time we find it is alongside heat-shattered handaxes and baked sediments." While the several distinct pieces of evidence make a strong case, figuring out if early humans lit flames on purpose is hard because the archaeological traces of natural and human-made fires look very similar. NASA / James Blair On October 31, four NASA crewmembers returned from “Mars.” Not the actual Red Planet, of course, but a 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston where the three men and one woman lived for 378 days. Now, the Mars analog astronauts— Ross Elder , Ellen Ellis , James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery —have started telling the world what took place after they disappeared into NASA’s Mars Dune Alpha habitat at the Johnson Space Center on October 19, 2025, for the agency’s second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission. The mission aimed to test the kinds of physical and mental conditions that a team of Mars explorers would endure on the Red Planet, including long-term isolation, disrupted communication with people on Earth and food cultivation. The habitat includes both a base and a mock outdoor environment , so the crew could practice Marswalks. “For more than a year, they have lived in an isolated environment, conducting critical research and helping us better understand what it will take to send humans to Mars,” Vanessa Wyche , director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, said during a livestream , just before the crew emerged. “Inside just 1,700 square feet, they managed to live with limited resources. The findings could be used to support the push to set aside half of Earth for nature , its authors say. “If you want to know where in the world you can find a place that has not yet been transformed by agriculture, infrastructure, or settlements, [this map] is where to find it,” says Erle Ellis, a global ecologist at the University of Maryland Baltimore County who contributed to the analysis. “There is a very strong consensus on where these places are.” The map, published today in the journal Global Change Biology, knits together four independently developed models for determining where humanity leaves its fingerprints, each using different indicators of activity. Museum Wales In 1999, Peter Hughes stumbled upon the brass combination lock on Margam Beach in Wales. It featured four rotating dials, each bearing six letters. The dials turned smoothly, but only one of 1,296 possible combinations would open the device. The lock was an artifact from the Ann Francis , a merchant ship that sank in 1583. Hundreds of the vessel’s treasures—including compasses, coins and cannonballs—have since surfaced on the beach. But Hughes was particularly intrigued by the lock. He fiddled with the dials for two decades, trying to solve the puzzle. Now, researchers have used CT scans to reveal the four-letter code: ANCE. It looked like a dinosaur vertebra at first. But upon further inspection, researchers realized the bone was a curved, sword-like crest that would have been attached to the skull of one of paleontology’s most oddball dinosaurs—the sail-backed predator Spinosaurus . “It was amazing,” recalls Vidal, of the University of Chicago. “It was like a unicorn.” Back in 2022, when he stumbled upon the strange bone, he was part of a team led by National Geographic Explorer Paul Sereno, a paleontologist also at Chicago , excavating a remote fossil site called Jenguebi. Now, the researchers report the crest belonged to an entirely new species— Spinosaurus mirabilis —that roamed the area’s ancient river ecosystem some 95 million years ago in the Late Cretaceous. They published their discovery Thursday in Science . The new species adds to a heated debate over how these puzzling (and popular) dinosaurs lived and hunted in water.

For centuries, the thermal springs have drawn visitors seeking healing, rest, and rejuvenation. Today, people come to soak in the water, drink it, and even sip beer brewed with it. After all, this is no ordinary water. What bubbles to the surface at Hot Springs National Park in Arkansas first fell as rain 4,000 years ago. Over the millennia, it seeped through thousands of feet of rock, warming as it went before faults and fractures in the sandstone channeled it back to the surface where now it gurgles up at 140° Fahrenheit. Long before Hot Springs was designated a national park in 1921, Native tribes, including the Caddo, Quapaw, and Osage, were drawn to its steaming waters. Beneath our cities, inside our hospitals, across our energy grids and beyond, complex networks of people and technology are working to keep the world moving. Threads of Connectivity is a mini-documentary series produced by Nicely Done Productions and narrated by Andy Serkis. Across 10 stories, it meets the people reimagining the infrastructure we rely on every day, revealing how extraordinary innovations are making our core systems stronger, smarter, and more connected. pages.text: Tiger Woods set for competitive golf return in December's Hero World Challenge - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Tiger Woods has won 15 major titles - three behind Jack Nicklaus' record tally By Timothy Abraham , BBC Sport Journalist and Michael Emons , BBC Sport journalist Published 4 hours ago Tiger Woods is set to return to competitive golf in December for the first time in more than two years. Woods, 50, has not played in a traditional ranking event since the 2024 Open Championship at Royal Troon amid a series of off-course issues. The 15-time major champion has endured a challenging few years with a number of injuries and turmoil in his personal life. Woods will host next month's Hero World Challenge - an event which is part of the PGA Tour schedule but does not carry FedEx Cup points - and has been announced as part of the 20-player field. The American is one of three exemptions for the tournament in the Bahamas along with compatriots Rickie Fowler and Gary Woodland. Speaking to SiriusXM PGA Tour Radio in a video posted last week, Woods said: "I'm feeling better, no doubt about that. "I've been training quite a bit. I will be at Hero either way, so I'll see you there." Woods' long-awaited return comes after he accepted a five-year driving ban in September following a plea agreement in his reckless driving case. In March, Woods had been arrested and charged with driving under the influence after clipping a truck and rolling his car in Florida.
